note: The ring of twelve lights, which turns level around Dante and Beatrice like a millstone.

context: A second circle of twelve wise souls forms around the first and matches its dance and song. Its members are named at the end of the canto.

note: Iris, goddess of the rainbow, who carries the messages of Juno, queen of the gods. The image is a double rainbow, the outer bow a reflection of the inner.
Echo. In Ovid's Metamorphoses she wasted away for love of Narcissus until only her voice was left, repeating what others say. The outer rainbow repeats the inner as an echo repeats a voice.

context: After the Flood, God set the rainbow in the clouds as the sign of his promise never to drown the earth again (Genesis 9).

note: Bonaventure, a Franciscan, who names himself at line 129. He speaks for the whole canto, as Thomas did in the last.
The magnetic compass, whose needle swings toward the Pole Star. It was still a fairly new instrument in Dante's Italy.
Dominic. The canto mirrors Canto 11 part for part: a Franciscan praises Dominic as the Dominican praised Francis, then rebukes his own order.
The Church on earth, pictured as an army. Arming it again after the fall of Adam cost the blood of Christ. By about 1200 it was straggling, weakened by heresy and by its own clergy.
Zephyr, the wind of spring, which blows from the west. The land where it rises is Spain, at the western end of Europe.
The Atlantic off the coast of Spain. For Dante no one lived beyond it, so the sun that sets there is hidden from all human eyes.
Dante's Italian has Calaroga: Caleruega, a village in Old Castile where Dominic was born about 1170. Calahorra, the name Longfellow used, is a different Spanish town.
The coat of arms of the kings of Castile and León is divided in four, with castles and lions. On one side the lion sits below the castle, on the other above it.
The enemies of the faith, that is, heretics. Dominic spent years preaching against them, and after his death the Dominicans were put in charge of the Inquisition.
According to the early lives, his mother dreamed while pregnant that she gave birth to a dog carrying a burning torch in its mouth, which set the world on fire.
Dominic weds Faith at his baptism, as Francis wed Poverty before the bishop in Canto 11. He promises to keep the faith, and the faith promises him salvation.

quote: the woman who had given her consent
note: His godmother, who answered for the infant at baptism. In the legend she dreamed of the child with a star on his forehead that lit the whole world.
Dominicus is the Latin adjective made from Dominus, "the Lord": it means "belonging to the Lord".

context: As with Francis in Canto 11, the name is held back until the story of the birth has been told.

note: In Dante's Italian the name Cristo ends this line and the next two rhyming lines. Throughout the poem Dante rhymes Cristo only with itself, as if no other word were fit to match it. This is the first of four such places in the Paradiso.

quote: the first teaching Christ had given
note: Usually taken to be poverty: "If you would be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor" (Matthew 19). Others think of the first Beatitude, "Blessed are the poor in spirit", or of humility.
The early lives say that as a small child he would leave his bed to lie on the bare ground, already drawn to a life of hardship and prayer.
The name is Latin for "happy" or "fortunate".
Medieval scholars explained the Hebrew name John, or Joanna, as "the grace of the Lord". The "if" allows that such derivations were not certain.

Dante names two men here: "the Ostian", Henry of Susa, cardinal bishop of Ostia and the leading writer on Church law, and Taddeo, probably Taddeo Alderotti, a famous Florentine professor of medicine. Law and medicine were studied for money, as in the opening of Canto 11.
The truth of God, the food of the soul. Dominic studied in order to know and teach it, not to make a career.
The Church, a common image from the Gospels. Its keeper is the pope.

context: Dante's Italian is in the present tense: the fault lies not with the papacy but with "him who sits there and goes astray", the pope reigning in 1300.

quote: two or three coins out of six
note: Three corrupt favors a churchman might ask of the pope. This is the first: leave to keep money owed to the poor and pay back only a third or a half of it.
A tithe is the tenth of income owed to the Church, meant largely for the relief of the poor. Dante gives the phrase in Latin, the language of Church law.
The Christian faith.
The souls of the two rings, twelve in each, all grown from the faith that Dominic fought for.
The pope's approval. Honorius III formally recognized Dominic's Order of Preachers in 1216.

Above all the Cathars, or Albigensians, of southern France, who held that the material world was the work of an evil power. Dominic preached among them for about ten years. Resistance was greatest around Toulouse.

context: The friars of his order, who carried his preaching across Europe.

note: The Church as a two-wheeled war chariot, with Dominic and Francis as its wheels. Dante saw the Church as a chariot in the procession on top of Mount Purgatory (Purgatorio 29).

context: Bonaventure turns from Dominic to his own founder, and to how badly the Franciscans now follow him.
He told the life of Francis in Canto 11.

note: The rut cut by the wheel's rim, that is, the path Francis marked out. His order no longer keeps to it.

quote: where crust once was, now there is mold
note: A proverb from the wine cellar. Good wine leaves a crust on the inside of the cask that helps preserve it; a neglected cask grows mold.

context: Bonaventure, once their head, accuses them of walking backward along their founder's path.

note: From the parable of the wheat and the weeds (Matthew 13): at harvest the wheat goes into the barn and the weeds are burned. The bad friars will find themselves shut out. Some see a reference to the pope's condemnation of the strict Franciscans in the years after 1317.
The Franciscan order, with each friar a page. A few pages are still as Francis wrote them.

context: For Bonaventure he goes too far in one direction, making the rule stricter than Francis wrote it.
He errs in the other direction, slipping out from under the rule.

quote: one avoiding it, the other narrowing it
note: The lax party escapes the rule and the strict party tightens it. Dante's Bonaventure condemns both extremes, as the real Bonaventure tried to hold the order together between them.
"Life" here means the living soul. Dante often uses the word this way for the blessed.
Dante's phrase is "the left-hand care": the business of money and power, which a churchman should keep in second place behind the care of souls.

Two early companions of Francis, not the great Saint Augustine. Illuminato of Rieti went with Francis to the Sultan. Augustine of Assisi was said to have died at the same hour as Francis. They stand for simple holiness among the scholars.

context: Mangiador is the Italian form of his Latin nickname Comestor, "the Eater".
His fame "shines below", on earth, in the twelve books of his handbook of logic. If he is Pope John XXI, he is the only pope of Dante's own lifetime whom the poem shows in Paradise.
A plain-spoken prophet among the scholars, perhaps placed here for his courage in telling a king the truth.

note: Grammar, meaning Latin, the first of the seven liberal arts and the door to all the others. Even the humble schoolmaster has a place among the wise.

context: In life Bonaventure opposed the Franciscans who followed Joachim's prophecies. In Heaven Joachim shines at his side, just as Thomas in Canto 10 stood beside his old opponent Siger of Brabant.
